claim: The AppNL-G-F/NL-G-F (App KI) mouse model expresses Aβ in young animals.
source: Here, we examined NPC and nucleoporin (NUP) distribution and nucleocytoplasmic transport using a mouse model of AD (AppNL-G-F/NL-G-F) that expresses Aβ in young animals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of the mouse model used in the study.

claim: Time-dependent accumulation of intracellular Aβ corresponds with a reduction of NPCs and NUPs in the nuclear envelope in App KI neurons.
source: Our studies revealed that a time-dependent accumulation of intracellular Aβ corresponded with a reduction of NPCs and NUPs in the nuclear envelope which resulted in the degradation of the permeability barrier and inefficient segregation of nucleocytoplasmic proteins, and active transport.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Reduction of NPCs and NUPs results in degradation of the permeability barrier in App KI neurons.
source: Our studies revealed that a time-dependent accumulation of intracellular Aβ corresponded with a reduction of NPCs and NUPs in the nuclear envelope which resulted in the degradation of the permeability barrier and inefficient segregation of nucleocytoplasmic proteins, and active transport.
evidence: This causal relationship is explicitly stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: App KI neurons become more vulnerable to inflammation-induced necroptosis as a result of NPC dysfunction.
source: As a result of the NPC dysfunction App KI neurons become more vulnerable to inflammation-induced necroptosis – a programmed cell death pathway where the core components are activated via phosphorylation through nucleocytoplasmic shutting.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Necroptosis core components are activated via phosphorylation through nucleocytoplasmic shuttling.
source: As a result of the NPC dysfunction App KI neurons become more vulnerable to inflammation-induced necroptosis – a programmed cell death pathway where the core components are activated via phosphorylation through nucleocytoplasmic shutting.
evidence: This mechanism is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The nuclear pore complex is vulnerable to disruption in various neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Collectively, our data implicates Aβ in progressive impairment of nuclear pore function and further confirms that the protein complex is vulnerable to disruption in various neurodegenerative diseases and is a potential therapeutic target.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the introduction.

claim: The nuclear pore complex is a potential therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Collectively, our data implicates Aβ in progressive impairment of nuclear pore function and further confirms that the protein complex is vulnerable to disruption in various neurodegenerative diseases and is a potential therapeutic target.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the findings of the study.

claim: The precise contribution of Aβ toward the aetiology of AD remains elusive.
source: While Aβ expression is known to disrupt different neuronal processes, the precise contribution of Aβ toward the aetiology of AD remains elusive (De Strooper and Karran, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Nuclear pore complexes function as gatekeepers for the movement of macromolecules across the nuclear envelope.
source: In the eukaryotic nuclei, nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) function as gatekeepers for the movement of macromolecules across the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Each NPC is an assembly of several hundred proteins comprised of more than 30 distinct nuclear pore subunits called nucleoporins.
source: Each NPC is an assembly of several hundred proteins comprised of more than 30 distinct nuclear pore subunits called nucleoporins (NUPs; Rout et al., 2000; Alber et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Core scaffold proteins of NPCs are extremely long-lived proteins with low turnover rates in non-mitotic cells.
source: The core scaffold consists of inner and outer ring NUPs, some of which are extremely long-lived proteins with low turnover rates in non-mitotic cells (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FG-Nups have shorter half-lives than core scaffold proteins.
source: These FG-Nups have shorter half-lives and can exist in different states, including liquid-liquid phase separation, which regulates the permeability barrier in NPCs (Celetti et al., 2020; Frey and Görlich, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The nuclear permeability barrier facilitates passive movement of small molecules and proteins less than approximately 40 kDa in molecular weight.
source: The nuclear permeability barrier facilitates passive movement of small molecules and proteins across the central channel of the nuclear pore (<~40 kDa in molecular weight), while larger-sized proteins must be actively transported by coupling with nuclear transport proteins that recognize nuclear translocation signals (Strambio-De-Castillia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Larger-sized proteins (>40 kDa) must be actively transported by coupling with nuclear transport proteins that recognize nuclear translocation signals.
source: The nuclear permeability barrier facilitates passive movement of small molecules and proteins across the central channel of the nuclear pore (<~40 kDa in molecular weight), while larger-sized proteins must be actively transported by coupling with nuclear transport proteins that recognize nuclear translocation signals (Strambio-De-Castillia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: NUP depletion experiments that degrade the permeability barrier often disrupt nucleocytoplasmic transport of proteins and RNA.
source: Many NUP depletion experiments that degrade the permeability barrier often disrupt nucleocytoplasmic transport of proteins and RNA (Harel et al., 2003; Walther et al., 2003; Boehmer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Deficits in NPC structure and function have been linked to neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Increasingly, deficits in NPC structure and function have been linked to neurodegenerative disorders (Li and Lagier-Tourenne, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In Huntington's disease, mutant huntingtin disrupts the nuclear envelope and sequesters critical nuclear transport factors such as RanGAP1 and GLE1 in the nucleus which impairs RNA export.
source: In Huntington's disease (HD), mutant huntingtin disrupts the nuclear envelope and sequesters critical nuclear transport factors such as RanGAP1 and GLE1 in the nucleus which impairs RNA export (Gasset-Rosa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: NUP62 and NUP88 nuclear aggregates have been detected in HD neurons, leading to a loss of the Ran gradient and aberrant nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: In addition, NUP62 and NUP88 nuclear aggregates have also been detected in HD neurons, leading to a loss of the Ran gradient and aberrant nucleocytoplasmic transport (Grima et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9ORF72 is the most common cause of sporadic and familial forms of ALS and FTD.
source: For amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), the hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9ORF72 is the most common cause of sporadic and familial forms of the disease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Expression of C9ORF72 repeat expansions caused nuclear envelope abnormalities, altered composition of NPCs, mislocalized NUPs, and nucleocytoplasmic transport deficits.
source: Work done in their lab and others collectively showed that expression of the repeat expansions caused nuclear envelope abnormalities, altered composition of NPCs, mislocalized NUPs, and nucleocytoplasmic transport deficits (Freibaum et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Coyne et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Studies of TDP-43 pathology in ALS/FTD uncovered links to the nuclear transport machinery, confirming that NPC dysfunction and defects in nucleocytoplasmic transport are hallmarks of the disease.
source: Interestingly, studies of TDP-43 pathology in ALS/FTD also uncovered similar links to the nuclear transport machinery, confirming that NPC dysfunction and defects in nucleocytoplasmic transport are hallmarks of the disease (Chou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Abnormal localization or activation of transcriptional regulators has been reported in AD neurons.
source: In AD neurons, abnormal localization or activation of transcriptional regulators has been reported (Chu et al., 2007; Jordan-Sciutto et al., 2001; Ranganathan et al., 2001; Parra-Damas et al., 2017; Boissière et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The nuclear transport protein importin-α1 was found aggregated in Hirano bodies in AD brains.
source: In addition, the nuclear transport protein importin-α1 was found aggregated in Hirano bodies in AD brains (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: NUP153 levels are reduced in mouse AD neural stem cells.
source: Meanwhile, in mouse AD neural stem cells, it was reported that NUP153 levels are reduced (Leone et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Phospho-tau interacts with FG-Nups to promote aggregation and its presence disrupted NPC function and nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: More recently, phospho-tau is shown to interact with FG-Nups to promote aggregation and its presence disrupted NPC function and nucleocytoplasmic transport (Eftekharzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Human iPSC differentiated neurons that carry an autosomal dominant mutation in tau showed higher phospho-tau levels, along with abnormal invaginations in the nuclear envelope caused by microtubule invasion.
source: In human iPSC differentiated neurons that carry an autosomal dominant mutation in tau, higher phospho-tau levels, along with abnormal invaginations in the nuclear envelope caused by microtubule invasion were observed (Paonessa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Little is known about the impact of Aβ on nuclear integrity and NPC function.
source: While hyperphosphorylated tau interacts with NPCs and impair nuclear function, surprisingly little is known about the impact of Aβ, if any, on nuclear integrity and NPC function.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: The App KI mouse model exhibits robust Aβ neuropathology.
source: In this paper, we examined the nuclear integrity and nucleocytoplasmic transport dynamics in an APP knock in mouse model AppNL-G-F/NL-G-F (App KI) that exhibits robust Aβ neuropathology (Saito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: No neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) have been reported in the App KI mouse model.
source: While Aβ pathology is robustly detected in App KIs, no neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) have been reported in this mouse (Saito et al., 2014; Saito et al., 2019; Sasaguri et al., 2017), nor did we observe elevated hyperphosphorylated tau in App KI neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and reference to experimental data.

claim: App KI neurons do not show elevated hyperphosphorylated tau.
source: While Aβ pathology is robustly detected in App KIs, no neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) have been reported in this mouse (Saito et al., 2014; Saito et al., 2019; Sasaguri et al., 2017), nor did we observe elevated hyperphosphorylated tau in App KI neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The basal levels of apoptosis and necrosis in App KI cocultures are low, showing no difference from WT neurons.
source: The basal levels of apoptosis and necrosis in App KI cocultures are low, showing no difference from WT neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: App KI nuclei show a reduction in the average signal intensity of NUPs compared to time-matched WT neurons from DIV 14-28 cocultures.
source: We performed volumetric quantification of three-dimensionally reconstructed nuclei from confocal images and observed a reduction in the average signal intensity of NUPs in App KI nuclei compared to time-matched WT neurons from DIV 14-28 cocultures (Figure 1A-B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: App KI nuclei show a reduction in the coverage of NUPs across the entire nuclei from DIV 14-28.
source: We also observed a similar reduction in the coverage of NUPs across the entire App KI nuclei (DIV 14–28; Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: A loss of NUP signal was observed in individual App KI neuronal nuclei in mice as early as 4 months.
source: Just like in cocultured neurons, we saw a loss of NUP signal in individual App KI neuronal nuclei in mice as early as 4 months (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: A reduction of NUP signal was observed in 13-month-old WT animals compared to younger animals, indicating an age-dependent decline of the signal over time.
source: Of note, we saw a reduction of NUP signal in 13-mo. old WT animals as compared to younger animals, indicating an age-dependent decline of the signal over time.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations from the data.

claim: The average number of NPC puncta per nuclei was reduced in App KI neurons across all time points examined (DIV 7-21).
source: We then used IMARIS to identify and quantify RL1 puncta and saw that the average number of puncta per nuclei was reduced in App KI neurons across all time points examined, including a subtle decrease in DIV 7 neurons which was previously undetected (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: App KI neurons have higher average distances between NPC puncta for all nearest neighbor calculations, suggesting that NPCs are more sparsely distributed in App KI relative to WT neurons.
source: We next performed nearest neighbor calculations for each NPC puncta and showed that App KI neurons also had higher average distances between puncta for all nearest neighbor (1, 3, 5, and 9) calculations, suggesting that NPCs are more sparsely distributed in App KI relative to WT neurons (Figure 1F, H-I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1F, H-I.

claim: The largest reduction in NPC counts and distribution in App KI neurons occurred when neurons matured from DIV 7-14.
source: Notably, the largest reduction in NPC counts and distribution in App KI neurons occurred when neurons matured from DIV 7-14 (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1G-I.

claim: The majority of RL1 fluorescent puncta on the nuclear envelope colocalized strongly with NUP98 (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r=0.9541).
source: We confirmed these studies with high-resolution confocal imaging by demonstrating that the majority of RL1 fluorescent puncta on the nuclear envelope colocalized strongly with NUP98 (Pearson's correlation coefficient, r=0.9541 Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both NUP98 and NUP107 had lower levels of expression relative to WT neurons in App KI cocultures (DIV 14–21).
source: In App KI cocultures, both NUP98 and NUP107 had lower levels of expression relative to WT neurons (DIV 14–21; Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The loss of NUP98 is sustained from DIV7 to DIV21 in App KI neurons.
source: While the loss of NUP98 is sustained from DIV7 to DIV21, the reduction of NUP107 levels occurs in DIV14 neurons and is sustained in DIV21 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations from the data.

claim: The reduction of NUP107 levels occurs in DIV14 neurons and is sustained in DIV21 neurons.
source: While the loss of NUP98 is sustained from DIV7 to DIV21, the reduction of NUP107 levels occurs in DIV14 neurons and is sustained in DIV21 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations from the data.

claim: IHC of brain sections from WT and App KI animals showed a decline in NUP98 and NUP107 levels in CA1 pyramidal neurons across all ages tested.
source: To complement cocultures experiments, IHC of brain sections from WT and App KI animals also showed a decline in NUP98 and NUP107 levels in CA1 pyramidal neurons across all ages tested (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Neuronal nuclei from 2-month-old App KI animals exhibit a reduction in NUP98 and NUP107 despite low numbers of Aβ plaques at this age.
source: Interestingly, neuronal nuclei from younger App KI animals at 2 months already exhibit a reduction in NUP98 and NUP107 despite low numbers of Aβ plaques at this age (Figure 5A; Saito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and a citation.

claim: APP/PS1 mice show a similar reduction in NUP98 and NUP107 levels in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: To further confirm that the altered NUP levels can also be detected in other Aβ-expressing mouse models, we performed IHC on forebrain sections of 4–5 months old APP/PS1 (APPSwe/PSEN1-A246E) mice and saw a similar reduction in NUP98 and NUP107 levels in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Immunoblotting of isolated nuclei from 2- and 14-month-old WT and App KI mouse forebrains confirmed the loss of NUP98 and NUP107.
source: Finally, we isolated nuclei from 2- and 14 months old WT and App KI mouse forebrains via density gradient centrifugation for immunoblotting to confirm the loss of NUP98 and NUP107 (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Protein levels and subcellular localization of LAMIN-B1, and the morphology of the nuclear envelope remained comparable between WT and App KI neurons.
source: We noted that protein levels and subcellular localization of LAMIN-B1, and the morphology of the nuclear envelope as defined by the sphericity index remained comparable between WT and App KI neurons, suggesting that the overall architecture of the nucleus is unperturbed in the mutant (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The overall architecture of the nucleus is unperturbed in App KI neurons.
source: We noted that protein levels and subcellular localization of LAMIN-B1, and the morphology of the nuclear envelope as defined by the sphericity index remained comparable between WT and App KI neurons, suggesting that the overall architecture of the nucleus is unperturbed in the mutant (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A diffuse intracellular Aβ can be detected in App KI mice as early as 2 months.
source: In App KI mice, a diffuse intracellular Aβ can be detected in animals as early as 2 months.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations from the data.

claim: In older App KI mice, there is an increase of punctate Aβ-positive aggregates in hippocampal neurons.
source: In older mice, there is an increase of punctate Aβ-positive aggregates in hippocampal neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was an increase in intracellular Aβ levels over WT neurons that parallels the reduction of NUPs as neurons mature from DIV 7–28.
source: Similarly, in neuron cocultures, there was an increase in intracellular Aβ levels over WT neurons that parallels the reduction of NUPs as neurons mature from DIV 7–28 (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment of App KI neurons with DAPT partially restored both the coverage and average intensity of NUPs in the nuclei relative to DMSO controls.
source: Our results using pan-NPC RL1 antibody labeling showed that treatment of App KI neurons with DAPT partially restored both the coverage and average intensity of NUPs in the nuclei relative to DMSO controls, suggesting that inhibition of γ-secretase activity halted intracellular Aβ accumulation and prevented further deterioration of the nucleus and loss of NUPs (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase activity halted intracellular Aβ accumulation and prevented further deterioration of the nucleus and loss of NUPs.
source: Our results using pan-NPC RL1 antibody labeling showed that treatment of App KI neurons with DAPT partially restored both the coverage and average intensity of NUPs in the nuclei relative to DMSO controls, suggesting that inhibition of γ-secretase activity halted intracellular Aβ accumulation and prevented further deterioration of the nucleus and loss of NUPs (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: DAPT treatment reduced the amount of intracellular Aβ which inversely correlates with the loss of NUP expression.
source: Importantly, we noted that DAPT treatment also reduced the amount of intracellular Aβ (Figure 3H) which inversely correlates with the loss of NUP expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Only neurons exposed to oligomeric but not monomeric or fibrillar Aβ42 showed a reduction in intensity and coverage of NUPs.
source: Remarkably, only neurons exposed to oligomeric but not monomeric or fibrillar Aβ42 showed a reduction in intensity and coverage of NUPs (Figure 3K–L) and a corresponding increase in intracellular Aβ (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3K-M.

claim: The accumulation of oligomeric Aβ42 in neuronal soma correlated with the loss of NUPs.
source: In agreement with our hypothesis, the accumulation of oligomeric Aβ42 in neuronal soma correlated with the loss of NUPs, thus directly linking the presence of the toxic form of Aβ with NPC dysfunction.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: In the presence of App KI conditioned media, WT neurons showed a robust loss of intensity and coverage of NUPs similar to that observed in the App KI control group.
source: We observed that in the presence of App KI condition media (WT +appm), WT neurons showed a robust loss of intensity and coverage of NUPs similar to that observed in the App KI control group (App KI +appm), implying that internalization of extracellular Aβ from the media is sufficient to reduce NPC levels (Figure 3O–Q).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3O-Q.

claim: Internalization of extracellular Aβ from the media is sufficient to reduce NPC levels.
source: We observed that in the presence of App KI condition media (WT +appm), WT neurons showed a robust loss of intensity and coverage of NUPs similar to that observed in the App KI control group (App KI +appm), implying that internalization of extracellular Aβ from the media is sufficient to reduce NPC levels (Figure 3O–Q).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the data shown in Figure 3O-Q.

claim: WT neurons incubated with App KI media showed an increase in intracellular Aβ which is presumably up taken from the extracellular environment.
source: Indeed, for these WT neurons incubated with App KI media, we recorded an increase in intracellular Aβ which is presumably up taken from the extracellular environment (Figure 3R).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3R.

claim: Expression of Aβ is sufficient to trigger a reduction in NUP expression in neurons.
source: Collectively, these Aβ coculture experiments strongly indicates that expression of Aβ is sufficient to trigger a reduction in NUP expression in neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: App KI neurons had a faster rate of EGFP fluorescence recovery after photobleaching compared to WT neurons.
source: However, relative to WT neurons, App KI neurons had a faster rate of recovery, suggesting that the cytoplasmic pool of unquenched EGFP and other similarly sized proteins can enter the nucleus more readily (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The cytoplasmic pool of unquenched EGFP and other similarly sized proteins can enter the nucleus more readily in App KI neurons.
source: However, relative to WT neurons, App KI neurons had a faster rate of recovery, suggesting that the cytoplasmic pool of unquenched EGFP and other similarly sized proteins can enter the nucleus more readily (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: A moderate increase in nuclear-localized 4xEGFP was observed in transfected App KI neurons under steady state conditions.
source: However, prior to time-lapse imaging experiments, we already observed a moderate increase in nuclear-localized 4xEGFP in transfected App KI under steady state conditions (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In WT neurons, there was no change in GFP signal throughout the duration of the time-lapse imaging experiment for 4xEGFP, indicating that the 4xEGFP was unable to enter the nucleus.
source: Results show that in WT neurons, there was no change in GFP signal throughout the duration of the time-lapse imaging experiment (~1 h), indicating that the 4xEGFP was unable to enter the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations from the data.

claim: GFP fluorescence steadily increased in App KI neurons over the duration of the 4xEGFP experiment, suggesting that the compromised permeability barrier allowed nuclear entry of high MW proteins normally sequestered in the cytoplasm.
source: However, unlike WT neurons, GFP fluorescence steadily increased in App KI neurons over the duration of the experiment, suggesting that the compromised permeability barrier allowed nuclear entry of high MW proteins normally sequestered in the cytoplasm (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: Elevated cytoplasmic NLS-4xEGFP signal was observed in transfected App KI neurons under steady state conditions.
source: Prior to FRAP, we imaged fixed neurons and observed elevated cytoplasmic NLS-4xEGFP signal in the transfected App KI neurons under steady state conditions, likely signaling a disrupted permeability barrier (Figure 4K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In WT neurons, there was no change in either cytoplasmic or nuclear GFP fluorescence for NLS-4xEGFP which remained largely confined to the nucleus after photobleaching.
source: In WT neurons, we saw no change in either cytoplasmic or nuclear GFP fluorescence which remained largely confined to the nucleus after photobleaching (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4K-M.

claim: There was a marked increase in cytoplasmic GFP with a corresponding decrease in nuclear GFP fluorescence after photobleaching of App KI neurons expressing NLS-4xEGFP, indicating a leaky nucleus that promotes aberrant nucleus-to-cytoplasmic movement of NLS-4xEGFP.
source: In contrast, there was a marked increase in cytoplasmic GFP with a corresponding decrease in nuclear GFP fluorescence after photobleaching of App KI neurons, indicating a leaky nucleus that promotes aberrant nucleus-to-cytoplasmic movement of NLS-4xEGFP (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4K-M.

claim: There is elevated CRTC1 in App KI nuclei compared to WT neurons under basal condition.
source: Under basal condition, there is elevated CRTC1 in App KI nuclei compared to WT neurons, an observation that aligns with the compromised protein compartmentalization in App KI neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The nuclear permeability barrier is compromised in App KI neurons that leads to an unregulated, bidirectional movement of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins across the nuclear membrane.
source: Overall, our experiments indicate a compromised nuclear permeability barrier in App KI neurons that leads to an unregulated, bidirectional movement of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins across the nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: A decline in NPC function and disruption in nucleocytoplasmic transport occurs during the normal aging process.
source: A decline in NPC function and disruption in nucleocytoplasmic transport occurs during the normal aging process (Mertens et al., 2015; D'Angelo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: App KI nuclei are leaky, with a higher proportion of low MW dextrans found in the App KI nuclei for both 2- and 14-month-old animals.
source: Indeed, our results indicated that App KI nuclei are leaky, with a higher proportion of low MW dextrans found in the App KI nuclei for both 2- and 14 months old animals, and with older animals showing a much stronger deficit (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The nuclei did not rupture during the extraction process as the high MW dextrans were equally excluded from WT and App KI nuclear isolates.
source: Reassuringly, control experiments indicated that the nuclei did not rupture during the extraction process as the high MW dextrans were equally excluded from WT and App KI nuclear isolates (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The nuclear permeability barrier is compromised in App KI animals and can be detected at initial stages of the disease in mice, prior to robust presence of Aβ plaques.
source: In short, we conclude that the nuclear permeability barrier is compromised in App KI animals as well as in vitro and the damage can be detected at initial stages of the disease in mice, prior to robust presence of Aβ plaques.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: GFP fluorescence recovered rapidly in the first 30 s in WT nuclei expressing NLS-4xEGFP, reaching a plateau within 60 s post-photobleaching.
source: For WT nuclei, GFP fluorescence recovered rapidly in the first 30 s, reaching a plateau within 60 s post-photobleaching (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Fluorescence recovery was delayed in App KI nuclei expressing NLS-4xEGFP, with a more gradual increase of GFP fluorescence over time, eventually matching WT levels of recovery after approximately 30 min post-bleaching.
source: In contrast, fluorescence recovery was delayed in App KI nuclei, with a more gradual increase of GFP fluorescence over time, eventually matching WT levels of recovery after ~30 min. post-bleaching.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations from the data.

claim: For the first 30 s, GFP fluorescence recovered approximately three times faster in WT compared to App KI neurons expressing NLS-4xEGFP.
source: An analysis of the slope of recovery indicates that for the first 30 s, GFP fluorescence recovered approximately three times faster in WT compared to App KI neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on analysis of the data.

claim: App KI neurons showed a distinct reduction in the average intensity and coverage of importin β1 (IMP-β1) signal around the nucleus.
source: ICC experiments on time-matched cocultured neurons showed a distinct reduction in the average intensity and coverage of importin β1 (IMP-β1) signal around the nucleus in App KI neurons that is dependent on maturity of the cocultures (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: The intensity of RanGAP1 was significantly lower in App KI neurons.
source: Apart from IMP-β1, the intensity of RanGAP1 was also significantly lower in App KI neurons (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: RanGAP1 is tethered to the NPC and is critical for Ran GTPase-mediated active transport of nuclear proteins.
source: RanGAP1 is tethered to the NPC and is critical for Ran GTPase-mediated active transport of nuclear proteins (Matunis et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A loss of both IMP-β1 and RanGAP1 will negatively impact the nuclear transport of proteins.
source: It is highly likely that a loss of both IMP-β1 and RanGAP1 will negatively impact the nuclear transport of proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Loss of NUPs in App KI neurons leads to a disruption of the nuclear import of NLS-proteins via the classical importin α/β1-mediated pathway.
source: Collectively, our data argues that loss of NUPs in App KI neurons also leads to a disruption of the nuclear import of NLS-proteins via the classical importin α/β1-mediated pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Recent reports in post-mortem AD brains and in animal models for AD have linked necroptosis as a potential cell death mechanism.
source: Recent reports in post-mortem AD brains and in animal models for AD have linked necroptosis as a potential cell death mechanism (Jayaraman et al., 2021; Caccamo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: TNF-α is well-linked to the pathophysiology of AD as the levels of TNF-α is significantly elevated in patients and in rodent models of AD.
source: TNF-α is well-linked to the pathophysiology of AD as the levels of TNF-α is significantly elevated in patients and in rodent models of AD (Jayaraman et al., 2021; Caccamo et al., 2017; Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Key components of the necrosome complex including RIPK3 and MLKL undergo nucleocytoplasmic shuttling and are thought to be activated via phosphorylation in the nucleus.
source: Several reports have shown that key components of the necrosome complex including receptor interacting kinase 3 (RIPK3) and mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL) undergoes nucleocytoplasmic shuttling and is thought to be activated via phosphorylation in the nucleus (Weber et al., 2018; Yoon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Phosphorylated RIPK3 and MLKL are exported to the cytoplasm where they contribute toward assembly of the necrosome complex.
source: Subsequently, these phosphorylated proteins are exported to the cytoplasm where they contribute toward assembly of the necrosome complex (Weber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: At 4.5 hr after exposure to TSZ (100 ng TNF-α), the number of WT and App KI neurons undergoing necroptosis was elevated, with mutant App KI neurons showing higher necroptotic cell death, compared to mock treated controls.
source: At 4.5 hr after exposure to TSZ (100 ng TNF-α), the number of WT and App KI neurons undergoing necroptosis was elevated, with mutant App KI neurons showing higher necroptotic cell death, compared to mock treated controls (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Exposure of cocultures to Necrostatin 1 stable (Nec-1s) abolished TNF-α-induced necroptosis.
source: To ensure that the TSZ cocktail is activating necroptosis, we exposed cocultures to Necrostatin 1 stable (Nec-1s), a specific inhibitor for RIPK1 activity which abolished TNF-α-induced necroptosis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: App KI neurons recorded a higher fraction of neurons undergoing necroptosis relative to WT controls across all TNF-α concentrations tested (0.1 ng – 100 ng).
source: As the results indicate, App KI neurons recorded a higher fraction of neurons undergoing necroptosis relative to WT controls across all TNF-α concentrations tested (0.1 ng – 100 ng).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on observations from the data.

claim: Only App KI and not WT neurons exhibited significant necroptosis at low TNF-α concentrations (0.1–1 ng), suggesting that App KI neurons are more sensitive towards low concentrations of TNF-α.
source: Moreover, only App KI and not WT neurons exhibited significant necroptosis at low TNF-α concentrations (0.1–1 ng), suggesting that App KI neurons are more sensitive towards low concentrations of TNF-α (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Under control treatment conditions where no TNF-α is present in the TSZ cocktail, both WT and App KI neurons showed comparably low levels of cell death.
source: Importantly, under control treatment conditions where no TNF-α is present in the TSZ cocktail, both WT and App KI neurons showed comparably low levels of cell death, whereas at the highest level of TNF-α tested in our study (100 ng), App KI neurons remained more vulnerable to necroptosis than WT neurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In the absence of external inflammatory stressors such as TNF-α, App KI neurons are stable and do not undergo necroptosis.
source: This suggests that in the absence of external inflammatory stressors such as TNF-α, App KI neurons are stable and do not undergo necroptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the data.

claim: A dose-dependent increase in pMLKL and pRIPK3 was observed in neurons stimulated with TSZ, with high TNF-α stimulated neurons showing stronger levels of phosphorylation compared to low TNF-α-treated neurons.
source: Overall, we observed a dose-dependent increase in pMLKL and pRIPK3 in neurons, with high TNF-α stimulated neurons showing stronger levels of phosphorylation as compared to low TNF-α-treated neurons (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: The dose-dependent increase in protein phosphorylation correlates with induction of necroptosis and agrees with the model that phosphorylation of MLKL and RIPK3 are important cellular events prior to necrosome assembly.
source: The dose-dependent increase in protein phosphorylation correlates with induction of necroptosis and agrees with the model that phosphorylation of MLKL and RIPK3 are important cellular events prior to necrosome assembly (Weber et al., 2018; Yoon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: High concentrations of TNF-α triggered the phosphorylation of MLKL and RIPK3 in both WT and App KI neurons when compared to mock-treated controls while only App KI neurons responded to low TNF-α concentrations.
source: We further observed that high concentrations of TNF-α triggered the phosphorylation of the component proteins in both WT and App KI neurons when compared to mock-treated (0 ng TNF-α in TSZ) controls while only App KI neurons responded to low TNF-α concentrations (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: App KI neurons are more susceptible to TNF-α induced necroptosis through enhanced phosphorylation of MLKL and RIPK3.
source: This provides compelling evidence that App KI neurons are more susceptible to TNF-α induced necroptosis through enhanced phosphorylation of MLKL and RIPK3.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Blocking nuclear import and export dampened TNF-α induced necroptosis by preventing the transport and activation of component proteins in the nucleus in Jurkat cells.
source: A previously published experiment in Jurkat cells established that blocking nuclear import and export dampened TNF-α induced necroptosis by preventing the transport and activation of component proteins in the nucleus (Weber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: For WT neurons, the inhibition of nuclear export with LMB reduced cell death, while App KI saw a similar but smaller reduction.
source: For WT neurons, the inhibition of nuclear export with LMB reduced cell death, while App KI saw a similar but smaller reduction (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The larger magnitude of decline for WT over App KI neurons in necroptosis levels indicates that LMB is less effective in inhibiting cell death in App KI neurons.
source: The larger magnitude of decline for WT over App KI neurons in necroptosis levels indicates that LMB is less effective in inhibiting cell death in App KI neurons (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: LMB blockade of nuclear export is less effective in App KI neurons due to the compromised permeability barrier allowing activated necrosome proteins to exit the nucleus and accumulate in the cytoplasm.
source: We posit that LMB blockade of nuclear export is less effective due to the compromised permeability barrier allowing activated necrosome proteins to exit the nucleus and accumulate in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the data.

claim: The individual fluorescence intensities of both pRIPK3 and pMLKL in the soma were unchanged between control and LMB-treated neurons for both WT and App KI neurons.
source: The individual fluorescence intensities of both phosphorylated proteins in the soma were unchanged between control and LMB-treated neurons for both WT and App KI neurons (Figure 7I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7I-K.

claim: Both pRIPK3 and pMLKL were enriched in the nucleus of only LMB-treated WT but not App KI nuclei.
source: We next calculated the nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios for pRIPK3 and pMLKL separately and found both proteins enriched in the nucleus of only LMB-treated WT but not App KI nuclei (Figure 7L), thus validating our hypothesis that the compromised permeability barrier is preventing efficient retention of phosphorylated proteins in the nucleus and allowing the proteins to enter the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: The compromised permeability barrier is preventing efficient retention of phosphorylated proteins in the nucleus and allowing the proteins to enter the cytoplasm in App KI neurons.
source: We next calculated the nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios for pRIPK3 and pMLKL separately and found both proteins enriched in the nucleus of only LMB-treated WT but not App KI nuclei (Figure 7L), thus validating our hypothesis that the compromised permeability barrier is preventing efficient retention of phosphorylated proteins in the nucleus and allowing the proteins to enter the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: GppNHp reduces necroptosis by inhibiting nuclear entry and subsequent phosphorylation of RIPK3 and MLKL.
source: While LMB hinders necroptosis by blocking activated proteins from exiting the nucleus, GppNHp reduces necroptosis by inhibiting nuclear entry and subsequent phosphorylation of RIPK3 and MLKL (Weber et al., 2018), a process that is also likely to be impaired if the nuclear barrier is compromised.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Incubation with GppNHp resulted in a reduction in necroptosis only in WT neurons.
source: Indeed, incubation with GppNHp resulted in a reduction in necroptosis only in WT neurons (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6G-H (note: likely a typo, should be Figure 7G-H).

claim: GppNHp significantly reduced the somatic levels of pRIPK3 and pMLKL in WT neurons.
source: ICC of TSZ-stimulated neurons treated with GppNHp showed that in WT neurons, GppNHp significantly reduced the somatic levels of pRIPK3 and pMLKL (Figure 7J–K) while no reduction was observed for pRIPK3 in App KI neurons (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7J-K.

claim: No reduction in pRIPK3 was observed in App KI neurons treated with GppNHp.
source: ICC of TSZ-stimulated neurons treated with GppNHp showed that in WT neurons, GppNHp significantly reduced the somatic levels of pRIPK3 and pMLKL (Figure 7J–K) while no reduction was observed for pRIPK3 in App KI neurons (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: There is a partial reduction of pMLKL in App KI neurons treated with GppNHp.
source: However, there is a partial reduction of pMLKL in App KI neurons (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: The efficacy of GppNHp in reducing phosphorylation of RIPK3 and MLKL is lower in App KI neurons due to the compromised permeability barrier which allows unregulated entry of non-phosphorylated proteins into the nucleus.
source: Overall, the differences observed between WT and App KI neurons supports our hypothesis that the efficacy of GppNHp in reducing phosphorylation of RIPK3 and MLKL is lower in App KI neurons due to the compromised permeability barrier which allows unregulated entry of non-phosphorylated proteins into the nucleus (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The loss of NUPs and degradation of the nuclear permeability barrier in App KI neurons is linked with an increase in neuronal vulnerability toward TNF-α induced necroptosis.
source: In summary, these experiments collectively link the loss of NUPs and degradation of the nuclear permeability barrier in App KI neurons with an increase in neuronal vulnerability toward TNF-α induced necroptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: High-resolution confocal microscopy revealed that the reduction of NUP expression corresponded with fewer NPC puncta that are distributed further apart on the nuclear envelope in App KI neurons.
source: High-resolution confocal microscopy further revealed that the reduction of NUP expression corresponded with fewer NPC puncta that are distributed further apart on the nuclear envelope, thus indicating a potential loss of NPCs in App KI neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Depletion of individual components of the Y-NUPs (i.e. NUP107, NUP160, NUP133, etc.) can trigger a domino effect on other NUPs, thereby reducing their concentrations, overall NPC density, and disrupting protein and RNA transport.
source: While the loss of a single NUP may not result in a total collapse of the nuclear pore architecture and function, several studies have shown that depletion of individual components of the Y-NUPs (i.e. NUP107, NUP160, NUP133, etc.) can trigger a domino effect on other NUPs, thereby reducing their concentrations, overall NPC density, and disrupting protein and RNA transport (Harel et al., 2003; Walther et al., 2003; Boehmer et al., 2003; Souquet et al., 2018; Siniossoglou et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: NUP98 is an essential component of the NPC as a knockout mouse displayed deficits in active transport of nuclear proteins and inefficient assembly of selected NUPs in the NPC.
source: Even though NUP98 is not a long-lived protein, it remains an essential component of the NPC as a knockout mouse displayed deficits in active transport of nuclear proteins and inefficient assembly of selected NUPs in the NPC (Wu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: NUP107 forms part of the outer ring sub-complex that tethers the genome and preferentially associates with active promoters.
source: NUP107 forms part of the outer ring sub-complex that tethers the genome and preferentially associates with active promoters (Gozalo et al., 2020), while NUP98 can function as a transcription modulator in the nucleoplasm by interacting with a variety of binding partners for gene activation and silencing, as well as being a tethering point for importins (Cho and Hetzer, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: NUP98 can function as a transcription modulator in the nucleoplasm by interacting with a variety of binding partners for gene activation and silencing, as well as being a tethering point for importins.
source: NUP107 forms part of the outer ring sub-complex that tethers the genome and preferentially associates with active promoters (Gozalo et al., 2020), while NUP98 can function as a transcription modulator in the nucleoplasm by interacting with a variety of binding partners for gene activation and silencing, as well as being a tethering point for importins (Cho and Hetzer, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: NUPs have been shown to perform extra-nuclear function such as assembly and function of primary cilia.
source: In addition, NUPs have also been shown to perform extra-nuclear function such as assembly and function of primary cilia (Obado and Rout, 2016; Endicott and Brueckner, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Expression and subsequent cleavage of mutant APP to generate Aβ is required for the reduction of NUPs in neuronal nuclei.
source: We show evidence the expression and subsequent cleavage of mutant APP to generate Aβ is required for the reduction of NUPs in neuronal nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Inhibition of γ-secretase activity prevented cleavage of mutant APP and generation of Aβ, which led to the partial restoration of NUP levels.
source: Inhibition of γ-secretase activity prevented cleavage of mutant APP and generation of Aβ, which led to the partial restoration of NUP levels.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Direct incubation of oligomeric, but not monomeric or fibrillar Aβ42 in WT neurons resulted in the loss of NUPs.
source: Direct incubation of oligomeric, but not monomeric or fibrillar Aβ42 in WT neurons also resulted in the loss of NUPs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Levels of intracellular Aβ correlates with the amount of NUP reduction in App KI neurons.
source: We also consistently observed that levels of intracellular Aβ correlates with the amount of NUP reduction in App KI neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Aβ is the primary driver for the loss of NUPs.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that Aβ is the primary driver for the loss of NUPs and there is a strong likelihood that accumulation of intracellular Aβ is partially responsible for causing this phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: There is a strong likelihood that accumulation of intracellular Aβ is partially responsible for causing the loss of NUPs.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that Aβ is the primary driver for the loss of NUPs and there is a strong likelihood that accumulation of intracellular Aβ is partially responsible for causing this phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Studies in humans, primates, and rodent models of the disease have demonstrated intracellular Aβ accumulation in AD brains.
source: In agreement with our observations, studies in humans, primates, and rodent models of the disease have demonstrated intracellular Aβ accumulation in AD brains (Iulita et al., 2014; LaFerla et al., 1997; Oddo et al., 2003b; Kimura et al., 2003; D'Andrea et al., 2001; Wirths et al., 2001; Takahashi et al., 2004), arguing for a key role of intracellular Aβ in causing the nuclear pore dysfunction during early stages of the disease.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Molecular studies have identified Aβ accumulation in late endosomes and multivesicular bodies that precede plaque deposition, arguing that this phenomenon is an early event in pathogenesis.
source: Some of these molecular studies have further identified Aβ accumulation in late endosomes and multivesicular bodies that precede plaque deposition, arguing that this phenomenon is an early event in pathogenesis (Gouras et al., 2000; Takahashi et al., 2002; Oddo et al., 2003a; Knobloch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Recent studies using several mouse models of AD showed faulty Aβ-laden autophagic vacuoles that coalesce around the nucleus, causing the formation of membrane tubules and intraluminal accumulation of fibrillar β-amyloid in the perinuclear space.
source: Recent studies from Lee et al., 2022 using several mouse models of AD showed faulty Aβ-laden autophagic vacuoles that coalesce around the nucleus, causing the formation of membrane tubules and intraluminal accumulation of fibrillar β-amyloid in the perinuclear space (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: An earlier study detected the presence of Aβ and APP-derived fragments in the nucleus and perinuclear compartment.
source: An earlier study also detected the presence of Aβ and APP-derived fragments in the nucleus and perinuclear compartment (Pensalfini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Aβ-induced lysosomal leakage from vesicular structures could release the contents of the lysosomes which includes Aβ and other proteases that may cleave NUPs.
source: While extracellular Aβ is internalized as endolysosomes and initially precluded from the nucleus, several studies have shown that Aβ-induced lysosomal leakage from these vesicular structures could release the contents of the lysosomes which includes Aβ and other proteases that may cleave NUPs (Ditaranto et al., 2001; Ji et al., 2002; Yang et al., 1995; Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Unconventional routes of entry for Aβ have been proposed, including a direct, energy-independent uptake of soluble Aβ via passive diffusion.
source: Apart from endocytosis, other unconventional routes of entry have also been proposed, including a direct, energy-independent uptake of soluble Aβ via passive diffusion (Kandimalla et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Extracellular Aβ, whether internalized or binding to cell surface receptors, can also indirectly impact NPCs by triggering damaging cellular cascades.
source: Finally, it is important to note that our experiments do not rule out that extracellular Aβ, whether internalized or binding to cell surface receptors, can also indirectly impact NPCs by triggering damaging cellular cascades (Takuma et al., 2009; Benilova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The longevity and stability of NPCs and nuclear transport declines during normal aging process, with several cell and animal model studies showing an age/time-dependent reduction in NPCs and nuclear adaptor protein complexes, or loss of nuclear integrity.
source: While there is increasing evidence that proteinopathies interfere with NPC function, the longevity and stability of NPCs and nuclear transport also declines during normal aging process, with several cell and animal model studies showing an age/time-dependent reduction in NPCs and nuclear adaptor protein complexes, or loss of nuclear integrity (Mertens et al., 2015; D'Angelo et al., 2009; Rempel et al., 2019; Toyama et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The decline in nuclear pore integrity occurs in WT neurons, and is accelerated in App KI neurons.
source: Our experimental data hints that the decline in nuclear pore integrity also occurs in WT neurons, and is accelerated in App KI neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Reports have shown an increase of intracellular Aβ in aged primary WT neurons.
source: Intriguingly, reports have shown an increase of intracellular Aβ in aged primary WT neurons, suggesting the possibility that the normal decline of NPC function may be linked to gradual Aβ accumulation during the normal aging process (Burrinha et al., 2021; Guix et al., 2012; Baker-Nigh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: The normal decline of NPC function may be linked to gradual Aβ accumulation during the normal aging process.
source: Intriguingly, reports have shown an increase of intracellular Aβ in aged primary WT neurons, suggesting the possibility that the normal decline of NPC function may be linked to gradual Aβ accumulation during the normal aging process (Burrinha et al., 2021; Guix et al., 2012; Baker-Nigh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as speculation based on cited reports.

claim: A general decline in nuclear function, because of normal aging, and exacerbated in the presence of Aβ, contributes toward neuronal loss and the emergence of clinical pathologies associated with AD.
source: As age is the biggest risk factor for many types of dementia, we speculate that a general decline in nuclear function, because of normal aging, and exacerbated in the presence of Aβ, contributes toward neuronal loss and the emergence of clinical pathologies associated with AD.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as speculation based on the findings.

claim: Several NPC subunits are extremely long-lived proteins with low turnover rates in mammalian brains and in cultured cells.
source: The second scenario is particularly relevant to long-lasting damage sustained to NPCs as studies have shown that several NPC subunits are extremely long-lived proteins with low turnover rates in mammalian brains and in cultured cells (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013; Cho and Hetzer, 2020; Mathieson et al., 2018; Dörrbaum et al., 2018; Rabut et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: mRNA expression of select NUPs, specifically a subset of the Y-NUPs that form part of the NPC scaffold are downregulated in adult worms and rodents.
source: In addition to its longevity, mRNA expression of select NUPs, specifically a subset of the Y-NUPs that form part of the NPC scaffold are downregulated in adult worms and rodents.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: NUP107 and NUP153 RNA is dispensable in adult worms as eliminating its expression did not impact viability.
source: Incredibly, NUP107 and NUP153 RNA is dispensable in adult worms as eliminating its expression did not impact viability (D'Angelo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: There is minimal NPC biogenesis in non-mitotic cells as replacing the core scaffold proteins in nuclear pores would require a complete disassembly of the entire NPC complex.
source: These studies collectively indicate that there is minimal NPC biogenesis in non-mitotic cells as replacing the core scaffold proteins in nuclear pores would require a complete disassembly of the entire NPC complex, something that regularly occurs in mitotic cells when the nuclear membrane is remodeled during cell division (De Magistris and Antonin, 2018; Morchoisne-Bolhy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: If Aβ expressing neurons accrue minor insults to the NPCs over time, the damage cannot be rapidly restored, and the cumulative impairments could eventually jeopardize cellular homeostasis with devastating consequence such as neuronal loss.
source: The fact that NPCs are stable structures with low turnover rates highlights a unique vulnerability for AD neurons: If Aβ expressing neurons accrue minor insults to the NPCs over time, the damage cannot be rapidly restored, and the cumulative impairments could eventually jeopardize cellular homeostasis with devastating consequence such as neuronal loss.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as speculation based on the findings.

claim: Subtle nuclear deficits already occur at very initial stages of AD.
source: Indeed, some of our experiments using the mouse model hint at the possibility that subtle nuclear deficits already occur at very initial stages of AD.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: This study along with others, continue to demonstrate common features of nuclear pore dysfunction, disruption in permeability barrier and nuclear transport in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
source: To summarize, this study along with others, continue to demonstrate common features of nuclear pore dysfunction, disruption in permeability barrier and nuclear transport in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a summary of the findings.
